demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson is about the kit's own rows, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: The agent, its calculators and check_args, in the code
demos.purpose: Three of commands/tests/test_desk.py's agent tests. In the first, the agent passes a cap of 40, which neither LV-07 nor the message writes: refused, no calculation, no "Worked out in code". The second sends a gratuity question to the statute desk with the Code on Wages, not the Code on Social Security, among the passages, and has the agent ask for encashable_days, which the statute desk does not hold: two refusals, one by the Code check and one as an unknown tool. In the third the model raises a 429, and the section is the direct answer under the same Meter. A scripted model plays the agent and a table plays rag-api, so no model is called. commands/agent-turn.sh, given arguments, runs them in ~/graph-venv, which it makes with the chat image's pins if it is missing; with OFFLINE=1 it needs no project. The same check, on what your lane's rag-api returns. The cell asks POST /v1/passages, as documind-ui-sa, the account on every company's roster, for acme's handbook passages on "earned leave encashed on exit": the retrieval the agent's search makes, with no model call. Then it runs check_args() on jn-03's question twice, with a cap of 60 and then 45. 60 is NP-03's notice days: when NP-03 is among the passages, 60 is a number the turn has read, but it is not in LV-07's words, so the check refuses it with "refused: cap = 60 is not written in LV-07 of a handbook passage this turn read: search for that clause and use the figure it states". 45 is accepted, found in LV-07 at its passage's place in the list.

demos.heading: Change it: delete the prompt's rule
demos.purpose: The rule is advice to the model; the check is code. Delete the rule, run the tests and two turns on your lane, then put it back. One sentence of the system prompt tells the model where a calculator's numbers may come from: "Give a calculator only numbers and dates written in the person's question or in a passage, as they are written there: it refuses any other. When a number you need is in neither, say which one is missing." Delete it, in your checkout only, and keep "Work every figure out with a calculator, never yourself." The deployed Desk is not touched: the change lives in your copy of services/chat/desk_agent.py, which the offline tests and make agent-turn import, and nothing here redeploys the chat service. First jn-03; then "I am an E3 and I am leaving. How many days of earned leave will be encashed?", which gives no balance. About Rs 1.7 to 2.3 a turn. What to read. Each encashable_days call's arguments, and what came back. Without the rule a model may try a number of its own more often: a balance for the second question, which gives none, or a cap from the wrong clause. Every such call comes back refused, in the check's words; for a balance nobody wrote: "refused: balance = 50 is a fact about the person that their message does not state: ask them for it". The model then asks for the missing number or answers without a calculation, and the figure check at the end says whether any figure in its words has no source. Whether this model tries a wrong number at all on the day you run it is the model's own behaviour; what the run shows is that none gets past the check. The rule makes a refused call less likely, which saves a model call. It was never what made the figure right.

demos.heading: One question, two arms, over REST
demos.purpose: jn-03 to POST /v1/desk as evalacme: the routed Desk, then one agent with every tool. An eval account may send arm in the body of POST /v1/desk; from anyone else the field is a 403, "arm is for the Desk's eval accounts (desk_eval)". Arm B is the Desk everyone gets. Arm Astar skips the classifier: the router takes the fallback decision, marked arm Astar, and the desk graph answers it with one agent whose retrieve may search any class the person reads, with all seven calculators. The cell sends jn-03 on each arm, in a session of its own, and prints what the arms differ in: each section's desk and mode, its tool calls and refused calls, each calculation with its arguments and where they were found, and the turn's model calls and limits.cost_inr.

demos.heading: Three arms on the same twelve rows, compared and combined
demos.purpose: Each row goes to POST /v1/route and to POST /v1/desk as its company's eval account, in a fresh session. On arm B the dev gates apply, as in lesson 10.4: 95% route accuracy and 90% recall for each desk. On 12 rows that means all 12 routed right: 8 of 8 handbook rows and 4 of 4 statute rows. One wrong route prints a FAIL line and make ends with Error 1, and the saved run and the report are written all the same. About Rs 13 to 17. Arm C: past the gate and the masking, a direct answer over the doc types the person may read, with no classifier and no calculator. Its report says its route column shows the gate and coverage only, so read its authority and correct rates first. A calculator row asks for a figure that neither its question nor its clause writes, so arm C's model must work it out in its own words, where the figure check can see it. About Rs 5. Arm C: past the gate and the masking, a direct answer over the doc types the person may read, with no classifier and no calculator. Its report says its route column shows the gate and coverage only, so read its authority and correct rates first. A calculator row asks for a figure that neither its question nor its clause writes, so arm C's model must work it out in its own words, where the figure check can see it. About Rs 5. Arm Astar: one agent on every row, lookups included, over every class the person may read, with all seven calculators. The most model calls of the three: about Rs 17 to 24. --compare reads two or three reports of one split, one arm each, on the same rows, and refuses anything else: two reports of one arm, no report of arm B, two splits, or rows that differ. For each arm it prints the correct and authority rates with their Wilson intervals, the desk turns' rupees and model calls, p50 and p95 latency, and the turns in agent mode with their calculator results and refused calls. Then it pairs B against each other arm row by row, through evals/paired.py: Newcombe's interval for the difference, the exact McNemar p, and a verdict read against the margin written there before any run, 3 points, on 8 October 2026. evals/combine.py reads the saved runs as the members of an ensemble, at Rs 0. For each answer row it prints which members were right, by the route eval's own verdict. On a row where any member ran a calculator, the members vote: each proposes the (calculator, value) pairs its answer's calculations hold, which code returned and no model wrote, and the proposal more members made than any other wins. The answer of the first member that made it ships as it stands. A member with no calculation proposes nothing, and a tie abstains: the row goes to a person, since a regulated figure is not settled by a coin. Then come each member's rate, the rows where all, some or none were right, the vote beside the best single arm on the rows it voted on, and the figure check, desk_calc.unsupported(), on every member's answer. Do it: the combiners on scripted members, offline. --selftest runs on scripted members of fig-01, with no model call. Two members' calculators returned Rs 2,40,000; a third writes Rs 2,10,000 itself. With --layers 2 it adds an arbiter, which picks one member's answer from an enum of their names and ships it word for word, and two layers of a mixture-of-agents aggregator, each reading every answer of the layer before and writing a new one. The vote and the arbiter only choose among the members' answers, so neither writes a figure of its own. The aggregator writes new text: this one averages the figures it reads and writes "About Rs 2,25,000", a figure no member computed, and unsupported() flags it at every layer. That is the mixture-of-agents pattern's cost on a regulated figure: every layer is a model writing again, so its figures need the same check as an agent's, while the vote needs no model call at all. --layers goes up to 5. On a lane the arbiter and the aggregator would be model calls of their own; the kit runs them scripted only. Do it: the three saved runs, combined.

steps.purpose: The vote and the arbiter only choose among the members' answers, so neither writes a figure of its own. The aggregator writes new text: this one averages the figures it reads and writes "About Rs 2,25,000", a figure no member computed, and unsupported() flags it at every layer. That is the mixture-of-agents pattern's cost on a regulated figure: every layer is a model writing again, so its figures need the same check as an agent's, while the vote needs no model call at all. --layers goes up to 5. On a lane the arbiter and the aggregator would be model calls of their own; the kit runs them scripted only. Do it: the three saved runs, combined.
